cultivar: Seed-grown bushes of Chinese and Indian origin planted in the late nineteenth and Soviet periods, plus Soviet-bred selections such as Kolkhida; many old plantations are semi-wild
processing: Orthodox black tea: withered, rolled (by hand or small machines in the new workshops), fully oxidised and dried; the Soviet-era factories ran mechanised lines and also pressed tile tea, while today's small producers make whole-leaf tea and sometimes a lightly smoked or sun-dried variant.
harvest_season: May to September, with the first May pick the finest and most expensive; a second summer flush is fuller and the autumn leaf plainer. Winters are cold enough that the bushes go dormant.
appearance_dry: Dark, loosely twisted leaves with some golden tips and stems, often uneven in size, with a sweet, dried-fruit and hay scent.
appearance_liquor: Bright amber to reddish brown, clear.
appearance_wet: Copper to dark brown leaves, medium size, soft.
taste_profile: Soft, sweet and low in tannin: dried fruit, honey and a hint of hay or wildflower, with a round body and a mild, slightly tart finish; stronger Soviet-style grades are plainer and more brisk.

brewing.notes: Western style, no milk needed; it is gentle enough to oversteep without punishment. Good whole-leaf lots also work gongfu style at 5 g per 120 ml with short steeps.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's harvest by the small producers, usually with the month or flush (May tea costs most) and the village on the pack; the larger brands sell blended, undated black tea all year and some of it includes imported leaf. It keeps well for two or three years but is not aged on purpose.
description:
Georgia was the tea garden of the Russian Empire and then of the Soviet Union. Tea was planted on the humid Black Sea coast in the nineteenth century and seriously from the 1890s, when the Chinese tea master Liu Junzhou set up plantations at Chakvi near Batumi; under Soviet rule the industry grew into a vast mechanised business that supplied most of the USSR's tea. Quality fell as volumes rose, the market vanished with the Union, and the plantations were abandoned to bracken and goats. What exists today is a revival: small producers, mostly in Guria and Samegrelo, picking old bushes and making orthodox tea by hand.

The bushes are a mix of seed-grown Chinese and Indian stock and Soviet selections, growing in a climate with warm wet summers and real winters, so the plants rest and the leaf is picked only from May to September. Many of the revived gardens are overgrown old plantations picked by hand, sold as 'wild' or 'forest' tea, and the processing is simple orthodox black: wither, roll, oxidise, dry.

The cup is characteristically soft: sweet, low in tannin, with dried fruit, honey and a hay-like note, and a gentle finish, nearer to a mild Chinese black than to Ceylon. It needs no milk and tolerates careless brewing. The old Soviet 'Gruzinsky chai' that older Russians remember was a plainer, stronger industrial tea, and a few producers still make something in that spirit, including pressed tile tea.

Buy it from a named small producer with the harvest month and village on the pack, since the May flush is the one to want; the supermarket brands sold as 'Georgian tea' are blended, undated and sometimes bulked out with imported leaf. Prices for the hand-made teas are modest for the quality, and the producers also make green, white and oolong-style teas from the same bushes.

If you drink it with Georgian food, it pairs with the honey-and-walnut sweets of the region; and a Georgian green from the same maker shows the other half of the country's tea tradition.
history:
Georgian black tea comes from the humid west of the country, around Guria, Samegrelo, Adjara and Imereti. The usual account has tea planted there under the Russian Empire, with a Chinese tea master at Chakvi near Batumi as the founding figure, followed by a very large mechanised industry in Soviet times that fell apart with the end of the USSR.

Small producers have since gone back to the old, partly overgrown plantations and make whole-leaf tea by hand. This outline is widely repeated, but the details and dates are thinly documented here and should be read with care.
